domain.name: Data Analyst
domain.description: From SQL and spreadsheets to statistical analysis and business intelligence.

skills.name: Spreadsheet Analysis
skills.description: Analyze data in Excel and Google Sheets using formulas, pivot tables, and lookups.

skills.name: SQL Fundamentals
skills.description: Query relational databases with SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, and aggregate functions.

skills.name: Descriptive Statistics
skills.description: Summarize data with mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation, and percentiles.

skills.name: Data Cleaning
skills.description: Handle missing values, duplicates, outliers, and inconsistent formats before analysis.

skills.name: SQL Joins
skills.description: Combine tables with INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, and self joins.

skills.name: Python for Analysts
skills.description: Use pandas and numpy for tabular analysis, aggregation, and reshaping.

skills.name: Exploratory Data Analysis
skills.description: Explore datasets to uncover structure, patterns, anomalies, and relationships.

skills.name: Data Visualization
skills.description: Choose appropriate chart types and design clear, honest visualizations.

skills.name: Inferential Statistics
skills.description: Draw conclusions about populations from samples using confidence intervals and sampling theory.

skills.name: Business Metrics and KPIs
skills.description: Track and interpret core business metrics such as revenue, retention, and engagement.

skills.name: SQL Subqueries and CTEs
skills.description: Write subqueries, common table expressions, and window functions for complex analysis.

skills.name: Hypothesis Testing
skills.description: Test statistical claims using t-tests, chi-square, and p-values.

skills.name: A/B Testing
skills.description: Design, run, and analyze controlled experiments to compare variants.

skills.name: Regression Analysis
skills.description: Model relationships between variables using linear and logistic regression.

skills.name: Tableau / Power BI
skills.description: Build interactive dashboards and reports with modern BI tools.

skills.name: Dashboard Design
skills.description: Design dashboards with clear hierarchy, useful metrics, and appropriate interactivity.

skills.name: Cohort Analysis
skills.description: Group users by shared characteristics and track behavior over time.

skills.name: Funnel Analysis
skills.description: Measure conversion through sequential steps and identify drop-off points.

skills.name: Customer Segmentation
skills.description: Group customers by behavior and value to guide targeting and retention.

skills.name: Data Storytelling
skills.description: Communicate insights persuasively to technical and non-technical audiences.

questions.prompt: In Excel, which function looks up a value in the first column of a range and returns a value from a specified column in the same row?
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP searches vertically down the first column and returns a value from a specified column in the matched row.

questions.prompt: What does a pivot table primarily do?

options.text: Summarizes and aggregates data by grouping rows into categories

questions.explanation: A pivot table groups rows by one or more dimensions and aggregates numeric values by sum, count, average, etc.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause filters rows AFTER aggregation?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: Which SQL aggregate function returns the number of rows in a group?
questions.explanation: COUNT() tallies rows. COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs in that column.

questions.prompt: Which measure is most robust to extreme outliers?
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value when data is sorted, so extreme outliers barely shift it.

questions.prompt: What does standard deviation measure?

options.text: The spread or dispersion around the mean

questions.explanation: Standard deviation quantifies how far values typically sit from the mean.

questions.prompt: You have a numeric column where 15% of values are missing. Which is the safest default treatment?

options.text: Drop every row with a missing value
Fill with the column mean or median

questions.explanation: Mean or median imputation preserves sample size and roughly maintains the distribution. Dropping loses data; 0 distorts the scale.

questions.prompt: A column contains the values 'NYC', 'nyc', and 'New York City' for the same city. What is the primary issue?
questions.explanation: The same entity appears with different strings, so grouping by this column will split one city into three categories.

questions.prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return?

options.text: All rows from the left table, matching rows from the right
Only rows that have matches in BOTH tables
All rows from both tables regardless of match

questions.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only rows where the join condition matches in both tables.

questions.prompt: Which JOIN keeps all rows from the left table even when there is no match on the right?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every left row; right-side columns become NULL when no match exists.

questions.prompt: In pandas, which method groups rows and applies an aggregation like mean or sum?
questions.explanation: groupby() implements the split-apply-combine pattern: split by key, aggregate, combine.

questions.prompt: Which pandas method returns the first 5 rows of a DataFrame?
questions.explanation: df.head(n) returns the first n rows (default 5). df.tail(n) returns the last n.

questions.prompt: In EDA, which chart best shows the distribution of a single numeric variable?
questions.explanation: Histograms bin a numeric variable and reveal shape, skew, and modality.

questions.prompt: A correlation of -0.85 between two variables means:
questions.explanation: |r| close to 1 means strong linear association; the negative sign means as one increases, the other tends to decrease.

questions.prompt: Which color palette is best for sequential numeric data?
questions.explanation: Sequential data should use a gradient that encodes magnitude perceptually.

questions.prompt: The main drawback of a pie chart is:

options.text: Humans compare angles poorly vs lengths

questions.explanation: Bar charts are easier to compare precisely because lengths are easier to judge than angles.

questions.prompt: According to the Central Limit Theorem, as sample size grows:

options.text: The sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal

questions.explanation: CLT justifies using normal-based methods on sample means even for skewed populations, when n is large enough.

questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a mean means:

options.text: 95% of the data lies in this interval
~95% of such intervals would contain the true mean over repeated experiments

questions.explanation: It describes the long-run coverage of the interval-building procedure.

questions.prompt: Which metric best captures whether users keep coming back to a product over time?
questions.explanation: Retention measures how many users return after their first interaction.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a vanity metric and an actionable metric?

options.text: Vanity metrics look good but don't inform decisions; actionable metrics guide specific actions
Vanity metrics only apply to revenue

questions.explanation: Vanity metrics (total sign-ups, page views) feel impressive but don't tell you what to do next.

questions.prompt: In SQL, what is a Common Table Expression (CTE)?

options.text: A named temporary result set defined with WITH that exists only for the query

questions.explanation: CTEs (WITH clause) let you name subqueries, improving readability and enabling reuse within a single query.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause computes a value across a window of rows without collapsing them?
questions.explanation: Window functions use OVER() to compute running totals, ranks, and moving averages while preserving each row.

questions.prompt: A p-value of 0.03 means:

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
Assuming the null is true, there's a 3% chance of seeing data this extreme

questions.explanation: p-values are conditional on H0 — not the probability that H0 is true.

questions.prompt: A Type I error in hypothesis testing is:

options.text: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive)

questions.explanation: Type I error = false positive. Type II error = false negative.

questions.prompt: What does statistical power mean in an A/B test?

options.text: The chance of detecting a real effect if it exists
The number of users in the test

questions.explanation: Power = 1 - beta. Higher power means a smaller real effect is more likely to be detected.

questions.prompt: The main risk of peeking at A/B test results daily is:

options.text: Inflated false positive rate due to multiple comparisons

questions.explanation: Repeatedly checking p-values without correction inflates Type I error.

questions.prompt: In linear regression, what does the coefficient for a predictor represent?

options.text: The expected change in the target for a one-unit increase in the predictor, holding others constant

questions.explanation: Each coefficient estimates the marginal effect of that predictor, holding all others fixed.

questions.prompt: When is logistic regression used instead of linear regression?

options.text: When there are too many features

questions.explanation: Logistic regression predicts class probabilities for binary or multiclass targets via sigmoid / softmax.

questions.prompt: In Tableau, what is the main difference between a dimension and a measure?

options.text: Dimensions are numeric; measures are categorical
Dimensions are categorical (group by); measures are numeric (aggregate)

questions.explanation: Dimensions slice the data; measures are quantities you aggregate.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first question to ask before designing a dashboard?

options.text: Which chart type is most colorful?
Who is the audience and what decision does the dashboard support?
How many metrics can we fit?

questions.explanation: Dashboards should drive decisions. Without a clear audience and decision, the layout becomes noise.

questions.prompt: Which principle should guide the visual hierarchy of a dashboard?

options.text: The most important metric is largest and top-left; supporting detail recedes
Use as many colors as possible

questions.explanation: F-pattern reading and clear contrast let the eye land on the KPI that matters most first.

questions.prompt: Why limit a dashboard to 5-7 primary metrics?

options.text: Cognitive load — too many metrics obscure the signal

questions.explanation: Humans process ~5-7 chunks at a time. Beyond that, viewers skim and miss the important changes.

questions.prompt: In a cohort retention curve, what does the x-axis typically represent?

options.text: Time since user signup (days, weeks, or months)

questions.explanation: Cohort analysis tracks each group over time since their shared starting event.

questions.prompt: A retention curve that flattens over time usually indicates:

options.text: A loyal core of users who keep coming back

questions.explanation: A flattening retention curve is a strong sign of a stable user base.

questions.prompt: In a funnel with steps 1000 to 500 to 200 to 50 users, which step has the largest drop-off?
The primary purpose of funnel analysis is to:

options.text: Identify which step loses the most users so you can focus optimization efforts

questions.explanation: Funnels localize drop-off — you fix the worst step first for the biggest conversion gain.

questions.prompt: RFM segmentation classifies customers by which three dimensions?
questions.explanation: RFM scores customers on how recently they purchased, how often, and how much they spend.

questions.prompt: Why is customer segmentation useful for retention strategy?

options.text: Different segments respond to different retention tactics

questions.explanation: High-value frequent buyers, at-risk users, and one-time buyers all need different interventions.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between a data story and a data report?

options.text: A story frames data around a decision; a report lists observations

questions.explanation: Stories open with a question and lead to an action. Reports are inventories of what happened.

questions.prompt: When presenting to executives, which opening works best?

options.text: The recommended action or headline insight first

questions.explanation: Lead with the punchline. Executives want the decision; supporting detail follows for whoever asks.
